questions.stem: A substance can only be transported against its electrochemical gradient by:
options: Primary active transport
Facilitated diffusion
Simple diffusion through the lipid bilayer
Passage through ion channels
questions.explanation: No official answer key for this exam — answers worked out from the course.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT an example of primary active transport?
options: Na⁺–glucose exchange
Ca²⁺ ATPases
K⁺–H⁺ ATPase
The Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase pump
questions.explanation: No official key — Na⁺–glucose cotransport is secondary active.

questions.stem: Concerning the ionic origin of the resting potential, which answer is FALSE?
options: The Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase pumps
Voltage-gated sodium channels
The Gibbs–Donnan equilibrium
The selective permeability of the membrane
questions.explanation: No official key — voltage-gated Na⁺ channels are closed at rest.

questions.stem: What is the meaning of the all-or-none law for the action potential?
options: The action potential is triggered for any stimulus intensity
The action potential stays the same at suprathreshold activation levels
The action potential changes amplitude depending on the stimulus
The action potential can be partially triggered

questions.stem: What are the characteristics of graded potentials?
options: They occur in any region of the cell
Their amplitude is independent of stimulus intensity
They are summable
They have an activation threshold

questions.stem: What characterizes voltage-gated ion channels?
options: They are always open
They are activated by changes in membrane voltage
They are selective for a single type of ion
They are mainly involved in protein synthesis

questions.stem: About chemical synapses:
options: The neurotransmitter diffuses from the presynaptic to the postsynaptic element through gap junctions
Synaptic transmission is unidirectional
There is a synaptic delay
The pre- and postsynaptic membranes are continuous

questions.stem: The routes of neurotransmitter elimination are:
options: Enzymatic degradation
Diffusion in the synaptic space
Reuptake by presynaptic elements
Reuptake by postsynaptic elements

questions.stem: Receptors:
options: Are only expressed at the cell surface
Allow intercellular communication
Bind ligands such as steroid hormones and neurotransmitters
Have a very weak interaction with their ligand
questions.explanation: No official key — receptors can be intracellular and bind with high affinity.

questions.stem: Postsynaptic potentials recorded at neuro-neuronal synapses are phenomena that are:
options: All-or-none
Propagated, always reflecting postsynaptic hyperpolarization
Gradable and summable
Reflecting changes in ion conductance at the presynaptic level

questions.stem: In a neuro-neuronal synapse:
options: The neurotransmitter is not always acetylcholine
Sodium entry into the presynaptic terminal causes neurotransmitter release
The neurotransmitter can cause depolarization of the postsynaptic element
The neurotransmitter can cause hyperpolarization of the postsynaptic element

questions.stem: Intracellular second messengers:
options: Transmit information toward the cytosol
Play a role in signal amplification
Are made of large molecules
cAMP is one of these second messengers
questions.explanation: No official key — second messengers are small molecules.

questions.stem: In the liver, adrenergic stimulation causes:
options: Gluconeogenesis
Glycogenesis
Lipolysis
Glycogenolysis

questions.stem: Muscarinic receptors:
options: Are dopaminergic
Are located in autonomic ganglia
Are stimulated by organophosphates
Are inhibited by atropine
questions.explanation: No official key — organophosphates inhibit acetylcholinesterase, indirectly stimulating muscarinic receptors.

questions.stem: The sympathetic system at the sweat glands:
options: Preganglionic fibers are short
Preganglionic fibers are cholinergic
Postganglionic fibers are cholinergic
Postganglionic fibers are adrenergic
questions.explanation: No official key — the sympathetic innervation of sweat glands is cholinergic.

questions.stem: Presynaptic α2 receptors of the sympathetic system:
options: When stimulated, they cause vasoconstriction
They are stimulated by excess noradrenaline
They are inhibited by acetylcholine
When stimulated, they cause negative feedback on noradrenaline secretion

questions.stem: In skeletal striated muscle:
options: Thick filaments are mainly made of myosin molecules
The sarcomere is the contractile functional unit
Each muscle fiber receives several nerve terminals from one motor neuron
The heads of actin contain the binding sites for myosin

questions.stem: Myosin is:
options: Made of 2 heavy chains and one light chain
Made of 2 heavy chains and 4 light chains
Its head contains 2 binding sites
Its head contains an ATP hydrolysis site

questions.stem: The thin filament: actin is
options: Made of 2 light chains and 2 heavy chains
Made of G-actin, troponin and tropomyosin
Made of F-actin and tropomyosin
Contraction is the sliding of thin filaments between thick filaments

questions.stem: During contraction:
options: ATP is needed for contraction but not for muscle relaxation
ATP resynthesis occurs only through oxygen-consuming mechanisms
The resting length is the length of the muscle in the body at rest
The heat produced during shortening is proportional to the force

questions.stem: At the neuromuscular junction:
options: Acetylcholine release is triggered by the arrival of the motor neuron action potential
The duration of action of acetylcholine is not limited
The end-plate potential is a local potential, gradable by spatial and temporal summation
Transmission can be blocked by curare

questions.stem: Concerning skeletal muscle metabolism, the energy used comes from:
options: Direct phosphorylation of ATP by creatine phosphate
Anaerobic glycolysis
Oxidative phosphorylation
Breakdown of carbohydrates and lipids

questions.stem: About the internal environment (milieu intérieur):
options: It is the interstitial fluid in which the body's cells bathe and live
It represents 1/3 of total body water volume
Its role is to supply the substances needed for cell function and remove waste toward excretory organs
It is an environment that is always constant and balanced
questions.explanation: No official key — it is regulated within limits (dynamic equilibrium), not strictly constant.

questions.stem: Concerning the body's fluid compartments:
options: Interstitial fluid represents 80% of the internal environment
Intracellular fluid represents 2/3 of total body water volume
Transcellular fluids are the main component of the internal environment
Plasma and interstitial fluid have nearly identical ionic composition and osmolarity

questions.stem: In the Gibbs–Donnan law, all conditions are correct except one:
options: Electroneutrality must be respected on each side of the compartments
The product of non-diffusible ions is identical on each side of the compartments
The sum of diffusible ions is higher in the compartment containing the non-diffusible ion
The protein concentration of plasma is higher than that of the interstitial fluid
questions.explanation: No official key — it is the product of the diffusible ions that is equal on both sides.

questions.stem: The properties of the tracer in the dilution method — it must be:
options: Non-toxic
Able to diffuse outside the space to be measured
Not modify tissue function and metabolism
Strongly eliminated and/or metabolized

questions.stem: The mechanisms of interstitial edema are:
options: Increased capillary hydrostatic pressure through precapillary vasodilation or increased post-capillary pressure
Decreased plasma oncotic pressure from hypoproteinemia
Increased capillary membrane permeability following inflammation
When reabsorption exceeds filtration

questions.stem: Apart from renal regulation, a positive water balance causes:
options: Extracellular hyperosmolarity
Extracellular hypo-osmolarity
Intracellular dehydration
Intracellular overhydration

questions.stem: The daily protein requirement:
options: Can be considered covered for a balanced nitrogen balance
Corresponds to about 1 g/kg/day
Depends on the biological value of dietary proteins
Is proportional to weight

questions.stem: Direct calorimetry measures:
options: The heat of combustion of foods
The thermal coefficient of oxygen
The specific dynamic action of foods
The caloric equivalent of oxygen

questions.stem: Basal metabolism:
options: Increases in hyperthyroidism
Is the energy expenditure of a worker per day and per square meter of body surface
Has a value close to 40 kcal/m²/h
Exclusively represents the energy cost of renal function
questions.explanation: No official key — it is measured at rest, not for a worker.

questions.stem: Postprandial extra heat:
options: Is independent of the nature of the food ingested
Increases when food is given intravenously
Represents an energy expenditure during the transformations of food before cellular use
Is greater when the diet is very rich in protein

questions.stem: An adult subject, 170 cm and 70 kg, consumed 1.5 liters of oxygen in 6 minutes during measurement of basal metabolism. We can conclude that:
options: Their basal expenditure is about 1746 kcal/day
Their basal expenditure per kg of body weight is close to 24.9 kcal
Their basal metabolism is calculated at an ambient temperature of 30 °C
Their basal metabolism is calculated fasting
questions.explanation: No official key — 15 L O₂/h × 4.85 kcal/L × 24 h ≈ 1746 kcal/day; /70 kg ≈ 24.9 kcal. Measured at thermal neutrality (≈ 20 °C clothed).

questions.stem: Concerning basal energy expenditure:
options: It is intended for muscular activity
It is intended for renal consumption
It is intended for irreducible vital functions
It is the amount of energy used during sleep

questions.stem: Which physiological process helps dissipate body heat when it is hot?
options: Vasoconstriction
Sweating
Shivering
Thermolysis

questions.stem: When body temperature drops, what can be activated to generate heat?
options: Vasodilation
Sweating
Vasoconstriction
Thermogenesis
questions.explanation: No official key — vasoconstriction conserves heat but does not generate it.

questions.stem: The total daily energy intake (TDEI) corresponds to:
options: The energy supplied by energy-yielding macronutrients
The energy supplied by energy-yielding micronutrients
The energy supplied by minerals and water
The energy supplied by carbohydrates, lipids and proteins

questions.stem: In clinical practice, to calculate an individual's total energy expenditure (TEE), one must:
options: Calculate resting energy expenditure (REE) by direct calorimetry
Calculate resting energy expenditure (REE) with validated formulas
Specify the individual's physical activity level (PAL)
Use the formula TEE = REE × PAL

questions.stem: A negative energy balance corresponds to:
options: Energy intake higher than energy expenditure
Energy intake lower than energy expenditure
Energy intake equal to energy expenditure
Weight loss

questions.stem: Among these proteins, which provide all the essential amino acids?
options: Red meats
Eggs
Pulses (dried legumes)
Soy
questions.explanation: No official key — soy is a complete plant protein; other pulses are low in methionine.
